title: Karna's Gift of the Armor

sources.citation: Karṇa — the Tragic Son of the Sun, §V 'Stripped of his armor: the kavacha-kuṇḍala'. Mahābhārata (Ganguli tr., sacred-texts.com), Vana Parva ~300–310.
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, 'Kuṇḍala-āharaṇa — Karṇa's Sacrifice' (Vana 300–309): Sūrya's dream-warning, Indra's beggary, the flaying gift, and the Vāsavī Śakti / Ekāghnī dart.

cast.role: Karṇa — son of Sūrya, the dānavīra
Indra — king of the gods, disguised as a brāhmaṇa

beats.summary: Karṇa is born clad in golden armor and earrings fused to his skin, invulnerable while he wears them.
Sūrya warns Karṇa in a dream that Indra will come disguised as a brāhmaṇa to beg the armor, and that giving it means death.
Karṇa refuses to be dishonored by turning away a supplicant; his fame as the supreme giver outweighs his life.
At midday sun-worship, Indra approaches disguised as an old brāhmaṇa and begs for the kavacha and kuṇḍala.
Karṇa cuts the armor and earrings from his own body; the wounds heal but he is now mortal.
Moved, Indra reveals himself and grants the Vāsavī Śakti, an infallible dart usable once — which fate makes Karṇa spend on Ghaṭotkaca.

variants: The dart is named variously Vāsavī Śakti / Vasava-śakti / Ekāghnī (Vana Parva ~308–309).
The corpus notes the tragic redirection: Karṇa hoards the once-only dart for Arjuna but is forced to spend it on Ghaṭotkaca in the Droṇa Parva night-battle, which secretly saves Arjuna.
